title: Chapter 28 — Building the Complete Ticket
intro: Delivery, installation, haul-away, accessories, protection — quoting like a professional means presenting the full picture, not hiding costs until the end.

sections.title: The Complete Ticket Is Honest Selling
sections.content:
Many salespeople quote the appliance price and then surprise the customer with delivery, installation, haul-away, accessories, and warranty costs at the end. That feels like a bait-and-switch — even when it is not intentional.

The professional approach is to build the complete ticket from the beginning. The customer should understand the total investment — not just the product price — before they make a decision.

This is not about inflating the sale. It is about setting accurate expectations. Customers who understand the full cost upfront are less likely to have sticker shock at the register — and less likely to feel deceived.

sections.title: Present Every Component as Value
sections.content:
Delivery is not a fee. It is professional handling of a heavy, expensive product that gets it safely into their home.

Installation is not an add-on. It is making sure everything works correctly, meets code, and does not void the warranty.

Haul-away is not an upcharge. It is removing the old appliance so they do not have to figure out how to get a 300-pound refrigerator out of their kitchen.

Protection plans are not a sales tactic. They are coverage that prevents a $3,000 problem from becoming a $3,000 loss.

When you frame every component as value, the customer evaluates it differently. When you present it as a hidden cost, they resent it.

sections.title: Quote Once — Quote Complete
sections.content:
The best practice is to present one complete number — the total — and then break it down component by component.

'Here is the full package: the refrigerator, professional delivery and installation, haul-away of your old unit, and five-year protection. The total comes to $3,800. Let me walk you through each part.'

That is transparent. That is professional. And it prevents the awkward moment where the customer thought they were spending $2,500 and the real number is $3,800.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating ticket building, ask:

Does the salesperson present the complete cost upfront — or reveal charges incrementally?
Do they explain the value of each component — or just list the prices?
Does the customer understand the total investment before being asked to buy?
Is the quoting process professional and transparent — or does it feel like a surprise?

A complete ticket is not a bigger sale. It is an honest sale. Customers who understand what they are paying for are more confident buyers.
